outline.chapter_title: Orientation to U.S. Protection Law: Asylum, Withholding, and CAT
outline.description: Introduces the statutory and regulatory framework governing humanitarian protection, the institutional actors, and the distinct remedies available. Establishes the vocabulary and core concepts students need before engaging the case.
subtopics: Statutory bases: 8 U.S.C. §§ 1101(a)(42)(A), 1158 (asylum), 1231(b)(3) (withholding), and regulations at 8 C.F.R. pt. 1208
Institutional structure: roles of DHS, IJs, the BIA, and the courts of appeals
Relief versus protection: discretionary asylum, mandatory withholding, and CAT protection
Core burdens and standards: preponderance for asylum eligibility; well-founded fear; more-likely-than-not for withholding and CAT
Derivative asylum and rider respondents; non-derivative nature of withholding and CAT

outline.description: Sets out the doctrinal elements asylum applicants must prove, how those elements interrelate, and how presumptions and burdens shift across them.
subtopics: Defining a refugee under § 1101(a)(42)(A): past persecution or well-founded fear on account of a protected ground
The three-part past persecution showing: harm rising to persecution; nexus to protected ground; by government or private actors the government is unable or unwilling to control
Well-founded fear: subjective and objective components; role of country conditions
Protected grounds: race, religion, nationality, membership in a particular social group (PSG), political opinion
REAL ID Act causation: “one central reason” and its application to mixed motives

outline.description: Explores the threshold between harassment and persecution, the role of cumulative harms, and how different types of harm (physical, psychological, economic) are treated.
subtopics: Persecution as a term of art: more than restrictions or sporadic threats; “offensive” harm
Assessing harm cumulatively rather than incident-by-incident
Threats alone: when are they insufficient, and what aggravating factors matter (specificity, imminence, repetition, capability, accompanying actions)?
Physical harm not required: the evidentiary challenges of proving severe psychological harm
Family-targeted threats and child-focused incidents: how they factor into the aggregate assessment
Comparative notes: varying circuit approaches to threats and psychological injury

outline.chapter_title: Causation and Nexus: Political Opinion, Mixed Motives, and Personal Disputes
outline.description: Examines the nexus requirement with emphasis on political opinion claims, distinguishing persecution from personal vendettas or criminal motives.
subtopics: REAL ID’s “one central reason” test and rejecting incidental, tangential, or subordinate motives
Political opinion: actual versus imputed; evidentiary markers in the record (persecutor statements; timing; comparative treatment)
Mixed motives: proving a protected ground amid criminal, economic, or personal disputes
When professional or personal entanglements (e.g., lawyering, business conflicts) eclipse protected grounds
Best practices to develop nexus evidence: persecutor declarations, social media, slogans, and contemporaneous notes

outline.chapter_title: Private Actors and the Government ‘Unable or Unwilling’ Standard
outline.description: Explains how persecution by private groups can qualify when the state cannot or will not provide protection, focusing on proof, reporting, and the futility/danger exception.
subtopics: Doctrinal test: government stopped or tried to stop the persecutors; government offered protection
Notice and opportunity to respond: importance of reporting to authorities
When failure to report is excused: proving futility or danger with record evidence
Evaluating government efforts: distinguishing isolated apathy from systemic inability or corruption
Country conditions as corroboration; leveraging human rights and rule-of-law indicators

outline.description: Covers the internal relocation doctrine, who bears the burden, and how adjudicators assess feasibility and reasonableness.
subtopics: Regulatory framework: 8 C.F.R. § 1208.13(b)(1) and (b)(3)
Burden-shifting: effect of establishing (or not) past persecution
Reasonableness factors: family ties, economic viability, safety, social/cultural barriers, and access to services
Evidence of persecutor reach and the significance of safe stays elsewhere within the country
Using country conditions and expert testimony to contest relocation

outline.chapter_title: Standards of Review and Appellate Procedure
outline.description: Sets out how courts review asylum denials, what records they consider, and how issue preservation shapes outcomes.
subtopics: Jurisdiction and scope: 8 U.S.C. § 1252; consolidated review
Substantial evidence review of BIA factfinding; deference on credibility versus sufficiency
Reviewing BIA decisions with reference to IJ reasoning
Issue preservation and waiver on petition for review
Harmless error and remand principles in immigration appeals

outline.chapter_title: Case Study: Canon Jimenez v. Bondi (10th Cir. 2025)
outline.description: Uses the Tenth Circuit’s decision as a vehicle to apply the doctrine: unpacking facts, procedural posture, and the court’s analysis on persecution, nexus, government protection, and internal relocation.
subtopics: Factual narrative: political activity, property dispute with an alleged narco-trafficking leader, threats labeled as “snitch” retaliation, and child-targeted incident
Procedural history: IJ credibility but denial; BIA affirmance; narrowed issues on appeal (asylum and withholding only)
Persecution analysis: threats and psychological distress assessed cumulatively yet found insufficient
Nexus analysis: criminal/professional conflict as the primary motive; political opinion deemed tangential
Government protection: minimal reporting; evidence of law enforcement actions against the property undermining claims of state complicity
Internal relocation: safe temporary move; unharmed family remaining in-country; threats limited to neighborhood
Withholding claim’s dependency on asylum findings (higher standard)
What additional evidence might have altered the outcome

outline.chapter_title: Particular Social Group and Political Activism: Framing Alternative Theories
outline.description: Explores how PSG claims intersect with political activism and social leadership, and the risks of underdeveloped alternative grounds.
subtopics: PSG requirements: immutability, particularity, and social distinction
Common PSG formulations in civic/political contexts (e.g., “social leaders”) and pitfalls
Preserving alternative protected grounds: briefing and record development
Imputed political opinion versus PSG theories in gang and cartel environments
Strategic pleading in mixed-motive settings

outline.chapter_title: Evidence, Credibility, and Corroboration: Building a Winning Record
outline.description: Translates doctrine into practice: what evidence moves the needle on each element and how to present it effectively.
subtopics: Corroboration expectations post-REAL ID: police reports, medical and psychological evaluations, affidavits
Documenting government inability or unwillingness: complaint receipts, follow-ups, ombudsman or prosecutor outreach
Nexus proof: persecutor statements tying harm to protected grounds; timing and comparator evidence
Internal relocation rebuttal: expert declarations, relocation failures, persecutor networks’ geographic reach
Child-specific evidence and UNHCR guidance on child persecution

outline.description: Places the Tenth Circuit’s approach alongside other circuits and BIA doctrine to illuminate national trends and fault lines.
subtopics: Threats-as-persecution: stricter and more permissive approaches across circuits
Private-actor persecution and the reporting requirement: how circuits assess futility and danger exceptions
Mixed-motive causation after the REAL ID Act: recurring fact patterns (gang extortion, whistleblowing, political canvassing)
BIA and Attorney General guidance: evolution and current status of the ‘unable or unwilling’ test
Forum selection consequences for asylum lawyering

outline.chapter_title: Withholding of Removal and CAT: Relationship to Asylum
outline.description: Clarifies how withholding and CAT differ from asylum in standards, scope, and evidentiary showings, and why asylum failure often—but not always—defeats withholding.
subtopics: Withholding’s higher probability standard and non-derivative nature
CAT’s separate elements: torture, state action or acquiescence, and non-refoulement
When withholding or CAT succeed despite asylum denial (e.g., discretion or nexus failures)
Strategic sequencing and fallback theories in removal defense

outline.chapter_title: Significance and Doctrinal Trajectory of Canon Jimenez
outline.description: Analyzes how the decision fits within Tenth Circuit precedent and national doctrine, and highlights takeaways for future litigants.
subtopics: Reaffirmation of a high bar for threats-only persecution in the Tenth Circuit
Clarifying mixed-motive analysis where criminal/economic motives predominate
Emphasis on reporting and evidentiary development for the ‘unable or unwilling’ prong
Internal relocation as a practical safety valve in neighborhood-confined threats
Implications for political canvassers and community advocates entangled with criminal groups
Open questions and areas for further development (imputed political opinion; systemic corruption proof; child-focused claims)

outline.description: Provides exercises and prompts to test application of doctrine and to encourage deeper analysis of evidentiary strategy and policy.
subtopics: Problem: A canvasser in a different region receives explicit partisan death threats accompanied by assault—persecution?
Problem: Reporting to a specialized anti-corruption unit versus local police—how does that affect the ‘unable or unwilling’ analysis?
Problem: Nationwide cartel with documented reach—can internal relocation still be reasonable?
Discussion: Drawing the line between whistleblowing on crime and expressing a political opinion
Discussion: The role of psychological expert testimony in meeting the persecution threshold
